1.goal: To name the situation before any audio: two people from the group already talking, and her coming in halfway.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask when she last came into a call or a conversation late and had to work out what had already been said.
Say out loud what today’s product is: not understanding everything, but what she does in the second she stops understanding.
1.expected: A concrete example, probably from school or from a game call.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about a class where the teacher went too fast.
1.challenge: Ask what it cost her: did she do the wrong thing, or just feel lost?
1.monitoring: Whether she frames it as her problem (“my English”) or as a normal feature of fast talk. It is the second.
1.evidence: Her example, and that she heard what the lesson is for.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: Who is on the call, and why she is listening before she speaks.
run: Give her time to read. Confirm two things out loud: this is the Thursday call from last week’s chat, and the professor has finally replied.
Do not preview any content. The prediction stage depends on her not knowing.
2.expected: She connects it to lesson 1 straight away.
2.support: If she has forgotten the chat, remind her of one thing only: nobody emailed the professor.
2.challenge: Ask what she expects the professor to have said.
2.monitoring: Whether she assumes a reply from a teacher is good news. It is not, here.
2.evidence: Her one sentence about what the two of them are sorting out.
2.transition: Move on when she says what they are deciding.

3.goal: To risk a guess before hearing anything.
3.interaction: T–S, one line on screen, then the first turn played once.
run: Read the line out loud and ask the question. Accept ANY guess; do not confirm or correct.
Then play the first turn once.
If you confirm her guess, she stops guessing on the next ones.
3.expected: She guesses that something is canceled. It is narrower than that, not off.
3.support: If she will not guess, offer two options and ask her to pick one.
3.challenge: Ask what she would do first if the plan really were off.
3.monitoring: Whether she tolerates not knowing, or needs certainty before she speaks.
3.evidence: Her prediction, for comparison after the first listening.
3.transition: Move on when she has guessed and heard it once.
exact: Is she about to say the plan is off, or that the plan just got narrower? Pick one.

4.goal: One whole listening, no transcript, for the two questions on the screen.
run: Play the ninety seconds straight through, no pausing. Read the two questions WITH her before you press play.
CCQ: did the professor approve the painting? (She did not say. She changed the scope: one detail, not the whole work.)
If she asks for the transcript, hold it until stage 5. The difficulty is part of the task.
4.expected: She gets the change of scope. The two jobs may come out as one.
4.support: If she is lost, play it again with no new questions.
4.challenge: Ask her what Nate is actually annoyed about.
4.monitoring: Where exactly she lost the thread. Note the timestamp: you will stop there in stage 6.
4.evidence: Her answers to both questions, and the point where she lost it.
4.transition: Move on when she has answered both, even partly.

5.goal: To separate what was said from what was implied, and to find what was never said.
5.interaction: S classifies, T checks, audio replayed in parts.
run: Play it again, stopping where she lost it. She classifies; you check.
The two items that decide this stage are the numbers: twelve not fifteen, and Saturday at nine not Sunday.
The one that was never said is the professor approving the painting. It is the comfortable reading, and it is not there.
5.expected: Answer key, item by item: The presentation is twelve minutes long -- they said it. The slides have to be uploaded on Saturday night -- they said it, at nine. The group has presented the wrong version of a file before -- they said it, as the reason for the folder rule. Nate is annoyed that the time was cut -- they implied it, with the sheet she sent in June. Priya does not trust the group to finish on time -- they implied it, by wanting the file the night before. Professor Okafor approved the choice of the painting -- it was never said. The two implied items are the hardest: annoyance and distrust are both said as facts.
5.support: If she hesitates, ask: what exact words made you think that?
5.challenge: Ask her what Priya has not said out loud about the group.
5.monitoring: Whether she hears attitude as well as content. Her Listening is 206; attitude is where the remaining work is.
5.evidence: Which items she got wrong, and whether she caught both numbers.
5.transition: Move on when she gets the item that was never said.

6.goal: That SHE formulates what separates a repair that works from one that does not.
6.interaction: S marks two of four, then T asks what they have in common.
run: Four lines on the screen. She marks the two that get the missing piece back.
Then ask: what do the two you marked have in common?
The answer you want, in her words: both name WHICH piece was missing. The others hand the choice back, and the other person repeats what mattered to them.
She may say that interrupting is rude. Answer it once and move on: on a call, the person asking is the person following.
6.expected: Answer key: Sorry, I didn’t catch all of that -- no, it does not say which part. Wait -- twelve minutes, or fifteen? -- yes, one word answers it. Could you possibly repeat what you were explaining? -- no, it names nothing and the register is off. Just to check I got that: the file goes up Saturday at nine -- yes, it says the piece back for confirmation. She will get the two right and find it hard to say why.
6.support: If she cannot formulate it, ask what the other two leave Priya to decide.
6.challenge: Ask her to rewrite the first line so that it works.
6.monitoring: Whether the politeness objection comes back. If it does, it will cost her the production stage.
6.evidence: Her formulation, and whether she raised the politeness question.
6.transition: Move on when she has stated the difference herself.

7.goal: The six repairs said out loud, at the right second.
7.interaction: T plays and stops; S produces the repair on the spot.
run: Play it again and STOP at the marked points. At each one she produces the repair, immediately.
If she waits until the end, go back and redo the point. Waiting for the end is exactly the behavior this lesson exists to replace.
Correct here, immediately and briefly. In stage 7 you stop correcting.
Say that again? will feel too short to her. Insist once.
7.expected: The short ones are the hard ones. The long polite ones come easily and are the wrong register.
7.support: If a repair does not come, give her the first two words.
7.challenge: Take the phrases off the screen and do two more stops from memory.
7.monitoring: Whether she stretches short repairs into sentences. That is the register target of the cycle.
7.evidence: Which repairs came out, and which she lengthened.
7.transition: Move on when all six have been said, however rough.

8.goal: A live call she joins uninvited: one thing repeated, one thing confirmed, one job chosen.
8.interaction: S speaks, T is Priya. The call is already running.
run: You are Priya and the call is running when she arrives. Speak fast on purpose, once, with a number and a time together.
THIS IS THE LESSON: she has to come in WITHOUT being invited. Do not ask “Stella, what do you think?” — that question does her job for her.
At the end, make her choose: which of the two jobs is she taking? “Whatever you need” does not count.
Do not correct during. Write it down and give it back in stage 8.
8.expected: The first interruption is the expensive one. After it, the rest come faster.
8.support: If she does not come in at all for a minute, pause and restart the scene, naming the rule again.
8.challenge: Add a second speaker by switching voices mid-call, so she has to track who said what.
8.monitoring: How many repairs she makes, whether she names the piece, and whether she chooses a job out loud.
8.evidence: Count of repairs, whether she confirmed anything, which job she took and how she said it.
8.transition: Move on when she has asked, confirmed and chosen, or at five minutes.

9.goal: To give back what you noticed and run the same audio faster with one repair only.
9.interaction: T gives two points, S listens again at 1.25 and repairs once.
run: Two things, no more: one that worked, one that did not come out.
Count the repairs out loud with her. The number is the evidence.
Then: same passage, a quarter faster, ONE repair allowed. She chooses which.
Do not add new content. Same task, one changed constraint.
9.expected: At speed she will want the number. The change of scope is the more valuable spend.
9.support: If she freezes, let her choose the repair before you play it.
9.challenge: Run it once more with no repair allowed, and ask what she would still be unsure about.
9.monitoring: What she spends the single repair on. It shows what she treats as essential.
9.evidence: Her choice of repair, and the count from stage 7, both for the record.
9.transition: Move on when the replay is done.

10.goal: To close on what she recognizes, and to say where the cycle goes next.
run: She marks what she recognizes. Do not argue with the marks.
Homework, out loud: the same call at full speed with no transcript, plus two links.
Next lesson: tell her these two are the pilot, and that what comes next is built on what you saw here.
Fill in the post-lesson record before you close.
10.expected: She will mark the checking line higher than the interrupting line.
10.support: If she marks everything high, ask which she would still not do with people older than her.
10.challenge: Ask which of the six she would use in a class at school tomorrow.
10.monitoring: The gap between what she marks and what you saw in stage 7.
10.evidence: Her self-assessment and your record, both written before the lesson ends.
